ACTING CHAIR ( Senator Grogan ): Welcome, everybody. Sorry for the late start. We had to deal with some administrative matters with the committee. Thank you all for waiting. I declare open this hearing of the Community Affairs Legislation Committee into budget estimates 2026-27. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land and pay my respects to elders past, present and emerging and also extend that respect to anyone in the room or joining us online today. The committee has fixed Friday 24 July as the date for the return of answers to questions on notice, and we'll ask senators to provide any written questions on notice to the secretariat by Friday 12 June.

Committee proceedings today will begin with the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing in outcome 4, which is disability and carers. I will be chairing today's estimates, substituting for Senator Dorinda Cox. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes responses to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance for questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operation or financial positions of the department and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth should not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and should be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate's order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

ACTING CHAIR: I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect.

I would now like to welcome Senator the Hon. Jenny McAllister, Minister for the National Disability Insurance Scheme, representing the Minister for Disability and the National Disability Insurance Scheme and Minister for Health and Ageing. Minister, would you care to make an opening statement?

Senator McAllister: I would, please.

ACTING CHAIR: Please go ahead.

Senator McAllister: Thank you, committee members. Given the extensive program of NDIS reform that the government has brought forward in the budget and the legislation that is currently before the parliament, I thought it would be appropriate to provide the committee with an update on the government's approach to these reforms. At the outset, I want to establish that the Albanese government remains committed to the long-term sustainability of the NDIS and to ensuring that it continues to provide life-changing supports for people with permanent and significant disability. The NDIS is a critical part of Australia's social infrastructure. It is a human rights achievement. It must be protected for people with permanent and significant disability and for the future. generations who will rely on it.

Minister Butler has announced this government's plan to fight fraud and stop rorts, to slow rapid cost increases, to apply clear eligibility and access requirements, and to deliver quality services and supports to participants. The NDIS amendment bill to secure the NDIS for future generations is currently before this committee, which I understand has received submissions and will be holding public hearings as part of its inquiry. I want to acknowledge that periods of reform and change can be stressful for community, and the prevalence of misinformation has exacerbated some of those concerns. I hope that we can use this forum today to engage in an informed discussion on the merits of the proposed reforms based on the facts that we have before us.

The committee has previously canvassed many of the issues related to fraud, non-compliance and integrity leakage currently within the NDIS. This government takes fraud seriously. Every dollar taken by fraud is a dollar taken from someone who needs it, and where we see fraud too often we also see a range of other harms to participants, from delivery of poor quality services through to abuse, neglect and exploitation. I know there are some in the community who are sceptical about the extent to which this government should be seeking to address fraud, but the evidence given to the Joint Standing Committee on the NDIS's inquiry into fraud was very clear. There is too much fraud in the scheme, and we are determined to address it.

Our position is that those who defraud the NDIS are stealing from the hundreds and thousands of Australians who rely on life-changing supports that the NDIS delivers. Our government is tackling fraud because it is the right thing to do so that all Australians can be confident that, should they rely on the supports provided by the NDIS, they will be provided with integrity.

A second tranche of reform measures seeks to return the NDIS to its original intent. The NDIS was established to support people with permanent and significant disability. Its scope has now expanded to cover many Australians with a diverse range of more moderate support needs. In part, this has been driven by a lack of available supports outside the scheme, whether we call these tier 2 supports or foundational supports. The lack of clarity about what supports are considered reasonable and necessary has also led to confusion, inconsistency and a broadening of supports funded by the NDIS over time. This divergence from the scheme's original intent has meant that the NDIS has grown at unsustainable levels.

The government has proposed a series of measures that will return the NDIS to its original intent. These include introducing a standardised evidence based assessment of a person's functional capacity to determine eligibility for the scheme; moving away from lists of diagnosis as a means of entry to the NDIS; clarifying the boundaries between the NDIS and mainstream service systems; and consistently assessing whether the NDIS is the appropriate system of support and if treatment could reduce or remedy an impairment. Many of these reforms are grounded in the observations and the recommendations of the NDIS Review, which engaged in extensive consultation with people with disability; their families, carers and advocates; and disability representative organisations, providers and support workers.

I understand that these are significant changes in how the NDIS has operated over the last decade. We are committed to working with the disability community, state and territory governments and other important stakeholders as we progress these changes, particularly those related to access to the NDIS. Part of our plans includes establishing a technical advisory group to provide advice to government on an appropriate threshold and approach to assessments for substantially reduced functional capacity. We would expect this group to work deeply with disabled people in the course of their work. These changes are alongside the introduction of new framework planning to deliver more equitable and consistent budgets for NDIS participants.

The third tranche of reform looks at the quality of services and supports available to participants. Current policy settings have not encouraged the transparency and innovation in NDIS services that we had expected at the beginning of the scheme. In many instances, rather, they have resulted in poor outcomes for participants, services of variable quality and, in some instances, viability challenges for providers.

The reform package includes a range of measures to address pricing and the design and delivery of core parts of the NDIS market, including plan management, support coordination and home and living supports. Our intention is to improve quality and encourage innovation and greater responsiveness to participant need. These measures include making the Minister for Disability and the NDIS the decision-maker on pricing; commissioning a panel of plan management providers to improve service quality and consistency and reduce fraud; and commencing consultation and design of a commissioning approach for home and living supports for participants who receive supported independent living.

The NDIS was built on the promise of inclusion. The vision of an inclusive Australia was a motivating construct in the final report of the disability royal commission, which recognised that inclusion is the opportunity for people with disability to live, learn, work, play, create and engage alongside people without disability. The individualised way in which the NDIS approaches social and community participation means that programs which once provided real opportunity for community connection have been allowed to wither away. We are establishing a $200 million Inclusive Communities Fund to rebuild the capability of community organisations to facilitate and enable genuine participation. I have committed to working closely with the disability community to design and deliver this capacity uplift.

We will also reset participant budgets for social, civic and community participation and capacity-building daily activities to 2023 levels. Social, civic and community participation remains central to the objectives of the NDIS and continues to be a critical part of participants' wellbeing and inclusion. We will also commence consultation on market reform of social, civic and community participation and capacity-building daily activities to ensure these supports are delivering their intended outcomes.

My final remarks are on the necessity of disability supports that sit outside of the scheme. The Albanese government is committed to ensuring all people with disability can access the supports they need. First ministers have come together at National Cabinet to sign a landmark agreement to invest an additional $10 billion in supports that sit alongside those delivered through the NDIS and through mainstream services. This investment is comparable to the entire expenditure on disability supports across all jurisdictions prior to the introduction of the NDIS in 2013.

Working with states and territories, the first $4 billion has been committed to establish Thriving Kids, a program of supports to help children with developmental delay and autism with low and moderate support needs, and to support their families and their parents. We want them to access those supports in a straightforward, timely manner in line with the findings of the NDIS review. This is a significant step in strengthening the system of disability supports outside the NDIS for people with disability across Australia.

Finally, I wish to thank senators and members across the parliament for their continued collegiality and for their collaboration. I think the community expects us to work across the parliament to ensure we are reaching the best possible outcomes for NDIS participants and the broader disability community.

ACTING CHAIR: Thank you. If you would table that, that would be great.

ACTING CHAIR: Mr Comley, welcome back. Do you have an opening statement?

Mr Comley : No, I don't, Chair.

ACTING CHAIR: Mr Head, do you have an opening statement?

Mr Head : No, I don't, Chair.

ACTING CHAIR: Ms Glanville, do you have an opening statement?

Ms Glanville : No, I don't, thank you.

ACTING CHAIR: Welcome also, Ms Wade. We'll start with Senator Steele-John.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: In fact, just taking account of the minister's opening statement, I'm going to modify some of my questions slightly. I'm happy to give the call to the opposition to begin.

ACTING CHAIR: Fantastic. We'll go to Senator Askew.

Senator ASKEW: Thanks very much for your time today. It's a long day ahead at the end of a busy week or two weeks. I'm going to start with staffing levels for both the NDIA and the commission, if that's okay. First of all, are you able to provide a breakdown of the staffing numbers for both the NDIA and the commission by APS level?

Mr Head : Yes. Just hold on one moment while we sort ourselves out.

Ms Glanville : I'm happy to start, if that's useful.

ACTING CHAIR: Thank you, Ms Glanville.

Ms Glanville : We have around 950 staff. Does that sound right, Laura?

Ms Sham : Yes. Data as at 31 March 2026 indicates we have 987 staff.

Senator ASKEW: FTE?

Ms Sham : Yes.

Senator ASKEW: Have you got that broken down by full time and part time?

Ms Sham : Yes, we do. At the APS EL2 level, it's 61; EL1 level, 216; APS6, 285; APS5, 258; APS4, 103; APS3, 21; legal special counsel, one; principal lawyer, which is EL2, four; senior lawyer, 11; lawyer, four; public affairs officer grade 3, five; and public affairs officer grade 2, two. Did you want me to provide the SES, which is also included?

Senator ASKEW: Yes, if you've got that.

Ms Sham : For SES band 1, it's eight; SES band 2, seven; and SES band 3, one.

Senator ASKEW: Excellent. Thank you very much. What are the NDIA numbers?

Mr Porter : As at 31 March 2026, in FTE terms, for APS2, it's 2.8; APS3, 442.8; APS4, 1,754.1; APS5, 2,862.7; APS6, 3,286.5; EL1, 1,436.9; and EL2, 626.4. In the SES we have 95 band 1s, 28 band 2s and eight band 3s.

Senator ASKEW: Have you got a total FTE there?

Mr Porter : Yes, it's 10,544.1.

Senator ASKEW: Thank you very much. Do you also have, by APS level, a breakdown of the staff vacancies in both the NDIA and the commission?

Mr Porter : For the agency, I don't have a breakdown with me, but we can get it for you during the break.

Senator ASKEW: If you wouldn't mind providing that on notice—or during the break would be even better—that'd be fantastic. On that, if there are vacancies, could you give me information on how long positions have been vacant?

Mr Porter : If we have that data in structured form, we're happy to provide it. I'll have to take that on notice.

Senator ASKEW: Thank you.

Ms Sham : For the commission, we'd need to take that on notice.

Senator ASKEW: The total number of vacancies as well?

Ms Sham : The commission is fully resourced. The only vacancies that we fill at this point in time are around attrition or where people have left roles.

Senator ASKEW: Okay. Are you expecting any changes to staffing levels due to the measures contained in the government's securing the NDIS for future generations bill, whether that be an increase or a decrease?

Ms Sham : The commission received 191 ASL provisioning, and that's to support the expansion of mandatory registration, as well as some support around expansion of our regulatory functions to support staff to do regulatory activities, and then general support for other measures underway.

Senator ASKEW: What sort of time will it be before that will be in place? A hundred and ninety-one is a fair few staff.

Ms Sham : Within the commission we had been operating slightly above our ASL level, so we are doing a recalibration at this point in time to ensure that we are positioning staff within the roles that will support those new measures.

Senator ASKEW: On the timeframe, once this legislation goes through, would it be three months or six months before you would be at full capacity again?

Ms Sham : I imagine that we would be at full capacity, certainly, within the first three months. That's really about the fact that there are some staff who will move, obviously, to support those new measures who already exist within the commission, as opposed to a large recruitment activity in order to staff up to that level.

Senator ASKEW: But you'd then need to recruit behind—

Ms Sham : That's right. We are preparing already to make sure that we will have the right complement consistently over the year, not just at one point in time.

Mr Porter : Like the commission, we have been operating slightly above our approved ASL levels. I've given you the FTE figures. The minimum ASL set out in the budget papers is 9,840, which is a contraction from our existing levels. I will point out that it is the minimum level and we are expecting some additional staffing to be approved alongside the release of funding. When approved, that's in the contingency reserve, again, as set out in the budget papers, for the delivery of the payment at point of support technology program.

Senator ASKEW: Do you have a number for how many that's likely to be, or are you saying it'll just be whatever's required?

Mr Porter : We're working through the DTA assurance process at the moment, and I'm not in a position to tell you what the number will be until that process has concluded. But the program is in the order of $353 million, so it is a significant program that will require a number of staff to deliver it.

Senator ASKEW: Do you have a rough idea of what you would expect that to be?

Mr Porter : I'm not in a position to tell you the number at the moment, but we're happy to take it on notice.

Senator ASKEW: I was going to ask: what is the timeframe before you would be in a position to provide that?

Mr Porter : I can't speak to how quickly other parts of government move.

Senator ASKEW: Fair enough.

Mr Porter : We hope that it will be as quickly as possible, but we of course need to go through the process ultimately to assure government that it will be an efficient and effective investment.

Senator ASKEW: If you could take it on notice to provide whatever you can around it, that would be appreciated.

Mr Porter : Of course.

Senator ASKEW: You're both working independently. Is there any likelihood that staff would be moving between the two—between the agency and the commission? Is what would happen as part of this rolling-out in relation to the legislation?

Ms Glanville : I can start. The agency and the commission work well together. Sometimes staff pick up jobs between the two and move from one to the other. That's not uncommon. It's one of the things I like about coming here to Senate estimates; I see a lot of staff from when I worked in the NDIA. It's fantastic that they're still here. So sometimes that happens; sometimes people decide they want to try what it's like with the administrator rather than the regulator. Personally, I would encourage that. It's good. It grows a stronger scheme. It enhances understanding of each other's roles and functions. Generally, it's a matter for people themselves. There's no formal plan in that way. Of course, we do work together very well. We both contribute staff to things like the Fraud Fusion Taskforce and those areas.

Senator ASKEW: It certainly does make sense—if you have a better understanding that way. I might move on to a different topic.

ACTING CHAIR: It might be a useful rotation point.

Senator ASKEW: I'll hand back to the chair.

ACTING CHAIR: Senator Steele-John, please go ahead.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: I put through an OPD in the last Senate sitting for a couple of key documents and figures from the government. I've got the OPD information back through that process. It appears to me that, if you add up a couple of the reforms that the government has framed as anti fraud, which are primarily—and, again, I'm interested in whether I've read this correctly—plan management and support coordination changes, particularly the commissioning pieces that you've spoken about; differentiated pricing for unregistered providers; mandatory registration; and ministerial decision-making in relation to pricing and fraud measures. If you pull those together, given the values you've assigned them in the OPD you've provided, we get to about $5 billion more broadly in terms of the overall amount that the government has forecast you will be cutting from the NDIS in the next four years or so. That total is $37.8 billion. So $5 billion of the $37.8 billion are attributable, in my interpretation, to measures that you framed as antifraud measures. Is that analysis correct?

Senator McAllister: I think the starting point, which is that all of these measures are antifraud measures, is not quite accurate. For many of the measures you refer to, the objective would be to improve the performance of the market. In the example of plan managers, there are some particular concerns we have about the role that some plan managers are playing in the system in relation to fraud. But the purpose of many of the other measures that you indicated is actually to improve the service quality or improve the cost-effectiveness of the market.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Do you have the OPD table in front of you that outlines the reform items and the amount of money that you intend to allocate to those in terms of the cuts and savings?

Senator McAllister: Indeed.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Alright. I just want to get this clear, because it's actually quite useful for the community more broadly. Where we've got item 3, for example—plan management and support coordination reforms—are you saying that it would not be correct to characterise that as an antifraud measure?

Senator McAllister: It is, but that is not its only objective, Senator.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Alright. If we go to, say, item 8—differentiated pricing for unregistered providers—would that be described as an antifraud measure?

Senator McAllister: Officials may wish to contribute to this, but principally, no, its purpose is not to address fraud; it's to improve the functioning of the market and to deliver better value and better-quality services for participants.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: If we look at the item about unregistered providers—would you describe a mandatory registration of providers as an antifraud measure?

Senator McAllister: Again, I think it has a dual purpose. You heard me say in my opening remarks that where we see fraud, we often see poor-quality services and, in the very worst cases, exploitation and abuse. Mandatory registration offers the opportunity to improve safeguarding and to improve the quality of services that are offered to participants.

Mr Comley : If I may just add on that one, to illustrate that point—Ms Glanville may want to comment—we probably think there are four main things that registration gives you. The first is genuine safety, potentially quality safety. The second is actually an overseeing of quality that are not necessarily safety but have other quality aspects. The third is market information—us knowing what's happening in the market. And the fourth is the category you're talking about, which is control of fraud. We would say registration can address all of those things.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: We have a budget where, as I said, you have forecast to cut about $38.7 billion from the scheme over the forward estimates. Based on your answers, we've got far less than about $5 billion of that overall amount of money directly attributable to antifraud measures, with the rest coming from cuts to plans, supports and services delivered to participants on the scheme rather than cuts actually impacting the large, fraudulent provider. Is that correct?

Senator McAllister: It's a good question, and I'm pleased you're asking it, because I am asked it often. When people assert that there are savings to government available from tackling fraud, they miss a key point. Mostly, what occurs when we tackle fraud is that the money being diverted away from participants who need those resources is returned to them. We intervene to deal with fraud and integrity questions, largely because we are concerned about the impact of those behaviours on participants. We intervene in those issues to deal with fraud, noncompliance and integrity because we think the community needs to retain confidence in the proper functioning of the scheme. You are correct in that, for the most part, there are not significant savings to government. There are some savings to government when we intervene, but mostly what occurs is an improvement of outcomes for people with disability who need support.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Going on what you've given today and the information of the OPD—you've confirmed to the parliament that there will be $38.7 billion cut from the scheme over the forward estimates and that less than $5 billion of that amount of money will come from anything that could be described as an antifraud measure, so the vast majority of what we've got here in this budget are cuts made to participants, impacting them rather than impacting the large private providers who are the primary perpetrators of fraud in the system. So we have a wildly disproportionate impact falling on people who are doing nothing wrong rather than falling on the large private providers who are doing something wrong. Your government is talking a lot about fraud in selling this legislation, but what you've just told me is that it's mostly about cuts to people's plans.

Senator McAllister: Your question misunderstands the evidence I've just provided. There will be very significant impacts on providers who seek to take money from people with a disability. That is the purpose of the fraud measures, and I can ask officials from the NDIA to step through those at a future point; we have many hours together. We do expect very significant impacts in this regard by way of the measures we're proposing. However, in terms of savings to government, intervening to prevent fraud, as I have already explained, generally returns money to people with disability who need it, not to consolidated revenue.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: In terms of talking about the dollars—

Senator McAllister: It's wrong to say that there will be no impacts on providers. That's simply not true.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Yes, but in terms of the dollars—because we're talking about the project; we're talking about people's funding. The vast majority of the cuts you're making are to people's services and supports, to therapies, to the support hours they need to leave the house to maybe connect with their community and to find and keep work. This is where the cuts are coming, and your own government's figures—the OPD information that I've just quoted to you—show that far less than $5 billion, which is not even 10 per cent of the overall value of the cuts that have been made in the budget, actually come from things that you would describe as anti-fraud measures. In fact, if I take you back to the OPD, the only one you were able to specifically describe that even mentions the word fraud is giving the minister the power to set pricing and take unilateral action in relation to fraud. Senator McAllister: Senator, your question incorrectly conflates two things. Mr Dardo : It's a very good question. It's an issue that we have to deal with in any government payment program. What you're describing there is the possibility that an entity has continued to operate under different ownership arrangements and with different representation. We just need to separate it out. I want to be really careful to talk about this at a macro level, not at a case level. There are circumstances where entities have appropriate legal arrangements in place to shut down a previous entity and to start a new entity. In some of those circumstances, they're perfectly acceptable and they're perfectly legal. They've done it the right way. If those things are visible to us, then, by law, we have to allow those things to happen.

There are circumstances where those arrangements are manufactured. They are arrangements to try and avoid previous liabilities. They are arrangements to avoid scrutiny. They are arrangements where they're hiding the real directorship, the real control, of the entity. We do have a maturing system. We started it with a very low base, but we're increasingly becoming sophisticated in detecting some of those arrangements. What I would say is, in some of those arrangements, you're not dealing with one—I'll use the term loosely—rebirth. You are dealing with a second, a third or a fourth rebirth. Senator BELL: With that example, where would be the appropriate place to report that kind of behaviour? If somebody thought something like that was going on, what would be the appropriate avenue to report that to resolve it?

We will share the intelligence with each other. We have different roles. I'll let the commission talk about what their role may be because the entity may be registered or unregistered. I'll let the commission talk about what they may do.

What we may do, from the NDIA perspective, is we may look for those things that indicate to us that this entity is not above board, and, if we find any indicators of those arrangements at all, then we have a range of interventions that we can apply. It wouldn't be obvious to members of the public if we had already applied those interventions. In some of those networks, we may have already executed search warrants on previous versions of that entity, but those interventions can include, at the most extreme end, search warrants and prosecutions. They do take time. We may be doing that without everyone being aware that those things have happened.

Manual payment reviews allow us to impose a position on an entity that says, 'You can't claim without us physically looking at every claim.' I would caution that a manual payment review is not something that you easily do without thought. I will explain why. It is true that some of these entities are awful entities. They're entities that we do not want in the market. The words that are being used by senators to describe some of these I think are apt words. But you've got to keep in mind that these entities may have participants, and they'll usually have a spread of participants. Some of those participants may be receiving partial genuine services or genuine services.

If we implement a manual payment review on an entity without working through the participant base, what they claim, where they're housed, what services they receive and what support they get, there is a risk that we will shut down all the services for 100 participants or 300 participants and have an adverse unintended consequence on the part of the participant base that is getting some genuine support.

Mr Dardo : Yes. We have approximately 170 types of risk detection in the system that allow us to surface risks associated with provider claiming.

Mr Dardo : We would generally not provide that because, as you can imagine, those are the keys to the kingdom. Those are the keys to the playbook to how we detect the fraud. But, included in that, are patterns of claiming.

We've got to be really careful. We may detect a pattern of claiming which is from one occasion or incidental. That may not get the same priority as systemic, volume and dollar figure patterns and safeguarding risk. We have to prioritise the interventions. Senator ASKEW: My questions are going to be about plan change requests and timeframes. Mr McNaughton, could you please provide the committee with an update on the processing times for plan change requests and how many were actioned within the 21-day timeframe, providing the numbers and the percentages of claims.

Mr McNaughton : In the nine months to 31 March 2026, we processed a total of—I can give you a breakdown of unscheduled reassessments and scheduled reassessments.

Senator ASKEW: I was coming to those, but, if you want to give me that upfront, that's great.

Mr McNaughton : We processed a total of 28,977 unscheduled reassessments that had a decrease in the plan, and 73,279 unscheduled reassessments had an increase in the plan. During the same period, we processed 22,653 scheduled reassessments that had a decrease in the plan and 20,126 scheduled reassessments that had an increase in the plan.

Senator ASKEW: How many of those were actioned within the 21-day timeframe?

Mr McNaughton : The 21-day timeframe is under our participant service guarantee.

Senator ASKEW: Those figures you've given me are the total number of plan changes that were done in those nine months.

Mr McNaughton : That's correct. Under the participant service guarantee, which is to decide whether to undertake a plan reassessment within 21 days, 29 per cent of those were within that 21-day period.

Senator ASKEW: How many is that in numbers?

Mr McNaughton : I'll get you the actual number that were in that time. What we do with that is apply a risk triage. It's not first in, first out. Some of those plan changes will be done in the same day or within 24 or 48 hours, depending on the risk triage they come in. Senator ASKEW: That makes sense. Of the 29 per cent that were actioned within the 21 days, how many led to the participant's change request being granted?

Mr McNaughton : Under the participant service guarantee, once we've made a decision to accept a plan request, we then have 28 days to process that. Senator ASKEW: On that, how many is that 87 per cent in the number of plans?

Senator ASKEW: And the same with the 29 per cent that were done within the 21—

Mr McNaughton : We can get that for you.

Senator ASKEW: For the ones that were declined, how many participants sought a review of the decision to decline the change request?

Senator ASKEW: If you could give me that on notice, that would be great.

Senator BELL: I want to move back to where we were before. I hope there are people who can still assist. Under those topics I was covering earlier, we looked at a few instances of operators allegedly billing for phantom care and banned operators reopening. Can the agency explain to Australians and taxpayers why, on the agency's own figures, fewer than 0.1 per cent of fraud tip-offs ever actually reached prosecution?

Mr Dardo : It is really important to understand the spectrum of interventions and behaviours that we need to deal with but also to understand the nature of tip-offs and how those tip-offs may trail into particular interventions. I might start at the tip-offs first. When we started the integrity improvement program four years ago, the tip-offs that were coming in were not codified in a way that was easy to interpret or understand. They had a lot of free text field in the tip-off. You could write what you wanted. It was difficult to understand where they were coming from and what the issue was and to put them in the system. There was no system that actually treated them in a way that we could analyse them.

Over the last four years we have invested significantly in completely revamping the way tip-offs are collected. We've codified the system. We now bring them and triage them into our platforms. We're able to connect those tip-offs to other multiple tip-offs. So we can now see that that particular tip-off relates to three previous tip-offs or relates to a case—an ongoing case, a previous case or a case in the pipeline. We can also codify it by the nature of the issue: was the tip-off from a staff member, was the tip-off from a provider staff member or was the tip-off from a participant and what's the tip-off about?

It's important to note that a tip-off, of itself, does not necessarily mean something that's bad has happened. In some cases, we look at the tip-offs and the tip-off is a misunderstanding that needs to be resolved, but it's not fraud and it's not malicious behaviour. It's not a bad thing. In some cases, we look at the tip-offs and it is an error. It might be on a participant's side or it might be on a provider's side.

Senator BELL: What percentage of tip-offs would you say is substantive?

Mr Dardo : The difficulty with describing that is that they get triaged for particular treatments and they get clustered up. As that happens, some of them may result in education interventions, some of them may result in a request for information to a provider or to a participant, some of them may result in a referral to another agency or to the commission and then some of them may result in criminal prosecutions.

Senator BELL: Is that something you can take on notice—what percentage of those clusters then proceed to further actions? You've just listed a number of actions there. If you could take that on notice—of those tip-offs, how many proceed through to those actions and any other additional actions? Is that something you can provide?

Mr Dardo : We can do that. What I would like to really highlight, though, is that the most important thing is to use the information from those tip-offs to ensure that safeguarding is happening—that there is a timely intervention for safeguarding if safeguarding is at risk—but to also bring an intervention to bear at the earliest possible time. In some cases, you don't need to get the prosecution because the matter is so light. You can intervene through education or through some other intervention.

Ms Wade : I think it's really important to highlight that, where there is a tip-off, the commission has a very specific and important response to ensure that the provider market is regulated effectively. I'll invite the deputy commissioner to speak to that.

Ms Myers : For tip-offs that we receive, we have a risk based prioritisation model. All of our tip-offs are assessed and, if required, referred to further processes within the commission. We look at what information holdings we have, what complaints we have and what reportable incidents we have, and we join up that information to make assessments of what action should be taken. Similarly to what Mr Dardo said, that could result in education or warning letters or go right through to a compliance inquiry or an investigation. It could lead to banning orders. It could lead to revocation of registration. There's a range of regulatory levers throughout the process.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: I want to ask Mr Fearnley some questions. Mr Fearnley, thank you for being here today and for your lifelong advocacy for the sector. Can you share with us what the board has undertaken, during your time as chair, in driving improvements in the participant experience?

Mr Fearnley : The board has restructured some of its subcommittees to ensure that we do get more participant voice into the board and the executive. We monitor the experience through our people and outcomes subcommittee as well where we're able to ask for more information and to challenge the agency, when it comes to participant outcome. We have also had Graeme Innes leading the audit and risk subcommittee. That does take into account the participant safety element of the scheme as well. I think a focus of the board has also been about really fighting for the voice of disabled people to be included in as many elements of the agency as we possibly can.

I would like to note—and it is a proud element of the agency and a focus of the board—that 23 per cent of our staff are disabled people. We want to be an employee of choice for disabled people, that they are able to feel like they are really valued members of the NDIA. I think we—me and Graeme Innes—even fought to keep that as a performance measure so that we are constantly held to account and to ensure that we do keep that representation of disabled people within the agency. The more that we can get disabled voices into lots of elements of the scheme, the better outcomes there will be for people with disabilities.

I'd also lean into the changes that have been made at the call centre, where we have seen great outcomes from the experience of participants when they call our call centre. From last count—again, it is within a percentage point or two—40 per cent of our call-centre staff are disabled people. That means that, when a disabled person calls with a question, there is that greater level of understanding. From memory, we had close to a 90 per cent satisfaction rate from people calling in to our call centre and feeling like their questions were answered satisfactorily, which is extraordinarily high across other government sectors as well.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: With your 23 per cent of staff, what's the distribution? Are they all the way through from grassroots up to middle management and above?

Mr Fearnley : We have representation of disabled people at every level of the agency now. In our senior leadership team, for the first time, over the last four years it's been 50 per cent of our board and, as mentioned before, at the call centre it's 40 per cent. We want to continually improve and we want to make sure that we are continuing to provide a workplace that is safe, that is welcoming and that values people of all experience of disability in the space that they are at.

Mr Innes : I'll add two small points, but I agree with everything that Mr Fearnley has said. The first is that that decision was made by the board at a recent board meeting in terms of keeping a performance accountability target of people with disabilities as a separate target to the other employment targets that we have. The second point is that, as well as the figures which Mr Fearnley has given you on disabled people, the agency also employs a significant number of people who are family members of disabled people. And so the figure is actually better than that 23 per cent if you broaden the grouping.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: Maybe on notice you could supply us with some of that data. I think that's interesting. What do you mean by 'performance accountability target'?

Mr Innes : There are certain targets adopted within the Public Service to ensure that the diversity of people in the community is represented. The target was proposed to be an inclusive grouping of various groups who experience disadvantage in the community. We chose to keep the number of people with disabilities separate to the other disadvantaged groups so that we would keep a stronger focus on that target.

Mr Fearnley : Just to clarify, 31 per cent of our internal staff identify as being disabled people. That's from the APS census in 2025. Also, our suppliers have hit their KPIs at 30 per cent for the call centre.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: Have you considered doing any outreach into corporate Australia to enable their workplaces to become more inclusive in the way that yours clearly is?

Mr Fearnley : I think a more inclusive Australia, not just across large and small businesses but also sporting clubs and community in general, is a much-needed process. The agency is a bridge to communities, but communities were also meant to lean into the agency so that people with disabilities can live a good life. I know that there are also matters before government about investing in a more inclusive community, and I would welcome more.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: I feel like that's a call to arms for the corporate CEOs, right? That's good.

Mr Fearnley : We will throw the challenge out there: come meet us at 23 per cent.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: We might too. I'm keen to draw you in on how you're thinking about AI. AI is a universe, right? But a lot of people are using AI queries for personal advice, sometimes companionship. There are safety risks; there are other kinds of issues. How are you thinking about AI both at an organisational level and how it's currently being used?

Mr Fearnley : I know that we do have an AI champion within the agency. You also want to have a participant-safety lens across this. But the opportunities that present itself for Australians with disabilities to live a good life are there. Graeme, I'm not sure whether you would like to touch on the use of technology and AI when it comes to glasses that are now used to be able to define the setting that you're in. It is an exciting time.

Mr Innes : The challenge with AI is that it brings significant advantages along with the disadvantages that you refer to. As Mr Fearnley has said, my personal experience is that I use AI in the glasses that I wear to describe images and to garner information as well as using AI in other areas of my work. But, as has been said, the agency has to keep a participant-safety lens on this. That's something that we're aware of both in terms the of use of AI internally in the agency and the use of AI outside it.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: What have those glasses done for your quality of life? It's interesting.

Mr Innes : Oh, they've made a significant difference to my quality of life. In our marriage, my wife used to be the only one who took the photos. That has now changed, which means that she's included in our family photos now when she wasn't in the past, and that's really important way for me to play a part in my family activities. That's just one example, but there is also just the information that I can gain. That's just one small example of the use of AI. There are many people with other disabilities and with similar disabilities to mine using AI to their benefit. But that's not to ignore the risks as well.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: Yes. We need to ensure we incorporate the voice of disability in any AI policy going forward. Thank you so much for that.

Ms Wade : Before you wrap up, just to compliment the evidence provided by the agency I just wanted to note that the commission has 22 per cent of people with disability that are represented in our workforce, and we are deeply committed to ensuring that we offer inclusive opportunities for staff across the commission contributing to the NDIS ecosystem.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: That's wonderful. Thank you for that contribution.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: My concern is that the royal commission made some 222 recommendations, 172 of those were within the Commonwealth's remit and, as of November last year, only eight of those recommendations had been implemented—that's two years after the royal commission had delivered its response—and yet we are hearing that the taskforce whose job it was to support and track the implementation was stood down. Senator McAllister: I think, as Ms Cassar was explaining, the function hasn't ceased. The department is still tracking and working to implement the recommendations. It's just that its natural home, organisationally, is with Australia's Disability Strategy.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: I've heard that response, but that division also has responsibilities other than the implementation and support of those particular recommendations. That's correct, isn't it? That isn't the only function of that division.

Ms Cassar : No, that's correct. It's not the only function of that division, but there is a very strong alignment in terms of the regular conversations that I and colleagues would have with other Commonwealth agencies around progressing action both under the strategy itself and on the disability royal commission recommendations. When we are thinking about actions that continue to progress, we also do make sure that, under Australia's Disability Strategy, we have at the forefront of our mind how they also intersect with the disability royal commission as well as the Closing the Gap targets.

Ms Glanville : Both mandatory registration and, particularly, SIL issues were raised as part of the royal commission, as you would know—

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Yes.

Ms Glanville : and those have been addressed and continue to be addressed. Particularly with SIL, there has been a lot of emphasis by the commission on that, and we've taken that on board. Definitely, the government has supported the commission in doing that important work and reaching the position we're at now.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: I hear that, thank you. Minister, your government has been talking a lot about the need to end violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect of disabled people. It is something that the Greens have been talking about for a very long time. There is a feeling in the community—and, I think, understandably—that sometimes when the government engages in these questions it is, more often than not, when it aligns with a broader political narrative, in this case a budget narrative, with a piece of legislation you're trying to pass. Now, whether or not you would think that's a fair characterisation, it is difficult to dispute when, more than two years on from the largest investigation of violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect ever conducted, we have eight recommendations implemented out of a possible 172 and the taskforce whose job it was to up that number is disbanded. You can understand why people would be quite cynical and more than a little bit affronted about that news, can't you.

Senator McAllister: My job is to make the best decisions that I can, to make progress on the things that matter and to listen to disabled people when they tell me what matters. I agree with you that the safety and the security and the protection of people with disability from violence is one of the issues people raise with me very frequently. It is specifically why I have, personally, brought great focus to advancing mandatory registration in the period that I have been the minister.

It is something that interests me in the context of the NDIS, because we have a lot of discussion about the NDIS and people's wish that it not be the only pathway for inclusion. Senator STEELE-JOHN:   I'll just push my luck with the chair once more. I did think that would be my last one. I hear that, Minister, but I would also state again that the political savviness of the disability community in Australia—

Senator McAllister: Unquestioned.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: and of our families is deeply present, and the royal commission meant so much to the community as an investigative body.

Senator McAllister: That's true.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: We're quite able to google the government responses to other royal commissions and then compare them to the way in which the government has responded to ours. People have shared with me a sense of real frustration and hurt that, when you look at, say, the government's response to the defence and veterans royal commission—not at all detracting from any of the legitimate community criticisms of either that commission or the government's response—what you did see there was the establishment of an implementation taskforce which ran until December 2025 and was not stood down until there was a permanent, legislated veterans commission, as recommended by the defence and veterans royal commission. Only at that point was that taskforce stood down. From the disability royal commission, there was also a recommendation for a disability commission that would then take over a lot of the functions of the taskforce, yet we have seen the taskforce stood down without the commission being in place and with only eight recommendations implemented by the government. That's the double standard that people see and that causes that hurt. I just think that needs to be clearly stated.

Mr Comley : I understand the concern of the community. From a Public Service point of view, on the allocation of resources, the vast majority of work that we do across the Public Service is not in taskforces. It's mainstreamed into areas, and we often do that to make sure it is mainstreamed and affects other activities. We bring taskforces together at various times, often because we want to bring disparate skills from other parts of the place, and it's easier to do it within one functional area. But I would just like to just make the comment that the existence or not of a taskforce is not a particularly good proxy at times for the amount of effort that's going into a particular area. I think that is what I would say to the community.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: The problem is that often, when we mainstream within bureaucracy, focus is lost. That might not be your personal experience, but it has been ours. ACTING CHAIR: Thank you, Senator Steele-John. We'll go to Senator Ruston.

Senator RUSTON: Mr Comley and Mr Head, before lunch, when I was questioning you, you said to me that the NDIA didn't know how many criminals—people who actually were in jail—were on the NDIS. I understand that back in 2024, the then minister for the NDIS, Bill Shorten, wrote to the states and territories asking for details on exactly that—how many criminals were on the NDIS. Mr Comley : I think I said I didn't know. That doesn't mean someone in the system doesn't know. But I see Ms Stengel is—

Mr Comley : Unless Mr Head wants to say something, we might go to Ms Stangel.

Ms Stangel : Senator, you're absolutely right. Following a section 55 request to all states and territories, which was made in around June 2024, all jurisdictions, except for one jurisdiction, provided data to the NDIS of participants that either had recently been or were being held in custody during that period of time for a 12-month period. We continue to work with the states and territories in being able to get a scheduled data set, to inform the agency when somebody is a current or prospective participant. The justice liaison officers, who are part of the Justice Planning Team, are face-to-face in working with nearly all correctional facilities across the country. So, through our justice liaison officers, we are aware very quickly about whether somebody needs access to the agency. That's one way in which we're able to collect data for people who may have access, or who are coming into the scheme. We also use a dataset from Centrelink which provides data matching. Centrelink data is a really great opportunity for us to understand when somebody is in and out of the justice system, and if they may be a NDIS participant. And we work extremely closely with the states and territories to refine that—obviously, there are local operational processes that work really well. Senator RUSTON: Okay. On the request from former minister Shorten for the states and territories to provide that data proactively: you're saying to me that the NDIA still does not have a dataset apart from the point-in-time data that you referred to. So there is no real-time requirement for the states and territories under that particular section, section 55, that you referred to?

Ms Stangel : That's correct. It's point-in-time data, but there is regular data sharing when requested.

Senator RUSTON: When is the last point-in-time data that you have taken from?

Ms Stangel : I'd have to take that on notice and get back to you.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. In the article which I'm having circulated, one of the reasons which former minister Shorten stated at the time was the fact that there was a lack of detail about serious offenders—particularly in relation to their monitoring requirements. There was the fact, as I said, that he didn't believe that the NDIS should pick up the tab for these people—and we're talking about serious criminals. He believed that the justice system should be. But it also—

Senator McAllister: I think that's quite a different issue, Senator Ruston. There have been some very significant operational changes to the way that we manage people upon release. It's a different issue that you're referring to. One of those—

Senator RUSTON: I'm actually talking about when they're in jail, not what you're talking about.

Senator McAllister: is that people who are on a high-risk offenders list are now agency managed, rather than self-managed.

Senator RUSTON: Yes, I know that.

Senator McAllister: You'll recall, of course, that under the Liberals people were self-managed in those circumstances. That's no longer the case.

Senator RUSTON: Thank you. I'm well aware of that.

Senator McAllister: Are you?

Senator RUSTON: Yes, I am absolutely well aware of it. It's a matter of many news articles, I might say. I understand that in that same correspondence—and I have to admit that I'm taking my comments from that news article—Mr Shorten also said that he was going to create a panel staffed by former law enforcement personnel to review applications and to provide advice before admitting people with a serious criminal history anywhere near the NDIS. I'm just wondering whether that panel was formed, and how often it meets?

Ms Stangel : Yes, that panel was formed. It has been in operation for about 18 months now. Just to be very clear, though: the members of the Justice Advisory Panel are not delegates of the agency, so they therefore don't make decisions about individual or prospective participants, or about NDIS plans. I just wanted to be clear about that. The panel is an expert advisory group which examines policy and systemic issues between state and federal government systems and that justice interface. Eligibility or planning, or any of the funding support decisions, remain with the NDIA delegates and not with the justice panel.

As I said, the panel commenced in 2024. It has held over 10 different bimonthly meetings to date. I have had the pleasure of being part of those panel meetings as well. Their tenure will be completed in August this year.

Senator RUSTON: To your point in terms of the role of this particular committee—as I say, I'm reading from a news article, but it does suggest that these are actually the words of the minister:

Shorten also announced in April the creation of a special panel staffed by former law enforcement personnel to review applications and provide advice "before we admit people with serious criminal history anywhere near our NDIS".

That doesn't really fit in with the role that you just described the advisory panel undertakes.

Ms Stangel : I certainly don't want to speak about the previous minister's response around that, but I'm only going by the delegation under the agency, which is that that panel members—and Kurt Fearnley was talking about IAC members—are not delegates of the agency and therefore cannot make a delegate decision in relation to eligibility or planning or funding. What they have done is, really, highlighted some key areas of systemic and policy issues that the agency needs to consider and think about. They are, at the moment, in the process of providing their advice through to the minister and the CEO. That is around their recommendations around the de-identified individual case studies that we've provided as evidence, as well as information to support them around high-risk offenders or forensic offenders that may be eligible or have been in the agency within the scheme. Some of their advice will probably be pointed towards some of the questions you've had around data sharing agreements. They've had significant workshops with our legal team within the NDIA and with our policy team, and they will have some further recommendations around how we might be able to manage that risk within the states and territories and the collaboration with the agency.

Senator RUSTON: If this panel is not making the decisions in relation to the admission of what they refer to as serious criminals into the system, who does make that decision?

Ms Stangel : We have a scheme eligibility branch that makes all access decisions for people, regardless of their criminal history or offending behaviour. The branch makes their decision based on the eligibility criteria. That hasn't changed. People still need to, obviously, meet permanency and reduced functional capacity criteria, as well as the other eligibility requirements, to be able to access the scheme. However, at that point in time, within access, it's not the role of the agency to consider a participant's offending behaviour or past behaviour. Our role is to make an access decision on somebody's disability support needs. That goes to planning as well. It's the role of police, justice and corrections facilities to manage or mitigate risk and safety concerns within the community. Our role is to make a reasonable and necessary decision about somebody's disability support needs.

Senator RUSTON: The thing that's concerning me a little bit about what you're saying is that we're two years on from the formation of this panel, 10 meetings later, and we still don't appear to have any formal advice from this group in relation to the very reason why the minister said that the group was going to be established.

Ms Stangel : I think it's fair to say that we've had ongoing internal advice through the panel meetings that have supported practice and process internally. In terms of formal advice back through to the minister or to the CEO, that is where we're at, at the moment, but there have been a lot of practice improvements and a lot of internal processes changes from some of the recommendations through the panel advisory.

Senator RUSTON: Is that internal advice able to be provided? I expect you'll probably take that on notice to seek advice—

Ms Stangel : I will take that on notice.

Senator RUSTON: but, if that internal advice from that committee in relation to how they have recommended these issues be addressed could be provided, that would be really useful.

Mr Carracher : I want to add that, from the commission's point of view, we've presented to the panel and had discussions with the panel on the use of lawful orders and distinguishing between lawful orders and restrictive practices under the rules in the NDIS. Senator RUSTON: Mandatory registration is something that obviously has been considered as part of the reforms going forward. I just wondered what modelling, assumptions and costings were used to deliver the cost figures contained in the budget papers?

Mr Comley : I'll ask Ms Long come to the table.

Senator RUSTON: I'm referring to the $182.6 million over four years and $46.1 million ongoing to introduce mandatory registration.

Ms Long : Was this in relation to the savings associated or do you mean the actual budget?

Senator RUSTON: I'm just interested in what modelling and assumptions sat behind coming up with that as the amount necessary. Is there any further background information?

Ms Sham : Ms Sham can address those questions.

Ms Sham : We modelled the cost for that to include components such as the actual stand up of registration, which is the policy enablement that would need to come into place in order to introduce mandatory registration for those categories of support.

Senator RUSTON: What does 'policy enablement' actually mean?

Ms Sham : That would be the development of the rules and the work to actually stand up the commission rules made by the commissioner to enable mandatory registration. The second part of that then would be actually facilitating readiness in the sector to understand what would be required of the sector, to become registered and to build understanding of compliance with the practice standards that will be expected of them through registration. The third part is actually registering providers. They will need to go through the registration process, which starts with an online suitability assessment and then moves through to audit to confirm their compliance against the practice standards. Then the final component is the ongoing expected regulatory actions that come from having registered providers. The compliance requirements include reportable incidents and obviously reporting that comes from having mandatory registration.

Senator RUSTON: So do you have the breakdown of each of these components that you've just outlined? I mean, how much of the $46 million a year goes to each of those components?

Ms Sham : I haven't got each categorised but I could provide that on notice. There is one other component. The other part of that was also the establishment of cost recovery, which will come into effect from 1 July 2027.

Senator RUSTON: Is that cost recovery in relation to registration?

Ms Sham : That's correct.

Senator RUSTON: So the cost of the registration will be recovered from the provider?

Ms Sham : That's correct.

Senator RUSTON: Don't start me on cost recovery. Will additional departmental staff be required to be hired to administer the mandatory registration changes that are proposed?

Ms Sham : There were 191 additional commissions ASL provided in the budget to support mandatory registration. I noted this morning in my evidence that the commission had been operating above ASL level, so we don't expect to have to hire 191 new staff. There will be staff within the commission that will be moving on to the new mandatory registration work.

Senator RUSTON: Over the period between 1 July 2027 and December 2030, which I understand is the period of time for this to be rolled out, how many new providers are you expecting to register in that time?

Ms Sham : There are approximately 80,000 providers that are delivering supports in those categories of services at the moment.

Senator RUSTON: Are they registered?

Ms Sham : They include a range of registered and unregistered providers because there's quite a lot of crossover in providers that may be delivering supported independent living, for example, or an existing registered category of support. Those providers will just need to add the new requirements for additional categories of support that they would be providing under mandatory registration. So there'll be a variation to their registration, not a brand new registration. But then there will be a range of unregistered providers who obviously will be new to registration.

Senator RUSTON: It would be really interesting to know the difference between those that are completely new to the registration process and those that have just got to do top-up.

ACTING CHAIR: When you're changing topic, we will rotate.

Senator RUSTON: Why is it necessary for such a long time? We're talking about 3½ years.

Ms Sham : In the introduction of registration it's important to get the right balance around moving towards not only having registration as a key component of the scheme and shaping the market but also making sure that that's not happening at such a speed that it potentially leaves such thin markets that participants would be unable to access those support services. So it's really about making sure we've got enough transitionary period to support the ongoing delivery of services within the market, while also transitioning providers to a registry.

Senator RUSTON: I'm interested in cost recovery. We've got a period of time of 3½ years where 80,000 providers will go through some level of activity, whether they be new or its existing providers. How are you going to manage the cost recovery arrangements during that time? Because until you've actually got the scheme up to full operation, you will only have the ability to amortise the cost of actually doing the registration over a smaller number of people. Is that going to be taken into account in terms of cost recovery, that they're not expected to fork out the whole lot of the cost of your administrative arm?

Ms Sham : That's right. We will work with the Department of Finance over the coming months to develop the cost recovery model. The way that that works in the cost recovery framework in government is that we need to be able to determine what is the efficient price and we only do that based on the activities of registration. It's not on other regulatory activities. It would only be the cost of facilitating the registration process for those providers, so that cost would be determined based on that year. Then it's revisited every year to make sure that we're getting the cost pretty much bang on to what it costs the commission to do that work.

Senator RUSTON: When does cost recovery come into play? When are you intending to bring it in?

Ms Sham : It's expected to come into play from 1 July 2027.

Senator RUSTON: So it's going to come in at the start of the program?

Ms Sham : From when advanced registration is expanded.

Senator RUSTON: Well, I'll look forward to the breakdown. When you provide the breakdowns of the five areas that you said, it'd be really good if you could profile it over the forwards.

Ms Sham : Yes, we can do that.

Senator RUSTON: Will there be scope for tiered registration of providers based on their service delivery type?

Ms Sham : That would be a question we're just working through at the moment to determine what's the most appropriate cost modelling to apply that. We will work that out over the next couple of months, to determine what's the right way to structure the pricing for fees, while ensuring that we are only cost recovering, obviously, the cost of actually doing the registration service.

Senator RUSTON: I'd be really interested to have a look at the agency's communication strategy is to make sure that providers understand their registration requirements, because, as you point out, we need to be very careful that we don't have participants being impacted by this change.

Ms Sham : That's correct.

Senator RUSTON: In the interests of time, if you could provide that communications plan on notice.

Ms Sham : Sure.

Senator RUSTON: Finally, in relation to registration, what conversations have been had between the commission and Ahpra in relation to registration? Have there been any discussions with Ahpra to ensure there's not a—
