ACTING CHAIR: Thank you. Senator Roberts.

Senator ROBERTS: I'd like to continue my line of questioning that I started on last time. Is the difficulty fraudulent claims by providers rather than by those with disabilities? I get the impression it's providers that are the big issue.

Mr Dardo : Overwhelmingly, when we see integrity issues, providers have a very significant role in those. I've previously raised in this forum on at least three previous appearances that those integrity issues can range across the spectrum in the way they interact with participants. The integrity issues may be that the provider has taken over the account of a participant that does not even know that the provider is abusing their plan. The participant has no idea; they don't know their identity or their plan is being used or compromised. We've been doing a lot of work to find ways to detect and stop that, and there is more work coming around that type of capability, but that is an example where a provider is doing things to a participant without the participant or the nominee even knowing.

Senator ROBERTS: And sometimes they eat up their whole plan's budget.

Mr Dardo : That used to be more easily done in the past. It is almost impossible to do now. We've got a lot more detection and controls around that now, but there are examples from four years ago where somebody's entire plan would disappear. They would not know that it had been spent, and it would disappear literally in the space of a couple of days. We have mechanisms now that detect those fast drawdowns. We put controls in place very quickly to do something about those fast drawdowns, to check with the participant or nominee from a safeguarding perspective and to protect the participant's plan.

There's a whole raft of controls that have been implemented over the last four years to stop that really malicious end of the provider behaviour. I would also emphasise that, in those cases, we've always taken a safeguarding approach. Once we identify that that plan has been drawn down without the participant or the nominee's consent the teams in the agency engage with the participants and nominees to put money back in the plan to ensure continuity of service so that those participants are not disadvantaged.

On the spectrum, the next level down from that would be that there may be providers that are taking advantage of very vulnerable participants. They are providers that have targeted a vulnerable cohort. The participants do not know that the arrangements they've entered into with the providers are problematic. The participants are highly dependent on providers. In the most extreme cases, we've worked with state police and other enforcement to intervene to address those behaviours by those providers. We've certainly shut a bunch of those providers down and we continue to do things to identify those. Again, the provider is the one at fault. In those circumstances, a vulnerable participant has been targeted. There are—

Ms Wade : Sorry, Mr Dardo. I wanted to add that, when the agency identify those sorts of plan drawdowns and that sort of behaviour, we have a very coordinated response to ensure that the provider is then subject to our regulatory intervention and that they are either banned from the market or subject to further enforcement action by us. It's really important that we do not have providers acting in that way. Certainly, for areas like the Northern Territory, where there are significant dependencies on service delivery that need to address vulnerabilities for cohorts, the commission has had a particular focus in the last little while.

Mr Dardo : This has been provided as testimony from other law enforcement agencies to the joint standing committee, but there are examples of providers that are facilitating a fraud in partnership with an individual. In those circumstances, we've got to be really careful to understand how much of that was coercion and how much was willing participation or inducement. Then there are some circumstances where the provider has been established by a trusted member, like a nominee or a family member, and that provider is defrauding the system. They fall at the smaller end of the spectrum. The bigger end of the spectrum is providers that are doing something without the participant's collusion, cooperation or awareness.

Senator ROBERTS: Has any thought been given, or has any action been pursued, with regard to increasing the penalties for those guilty of rorting the system? Because someone rorting the system is stealing from the disabled, as well as from the taxpayer.

Mr Dardo : Absolutely. I'll throw to the commission in a moment to talk about some of the consequences that exist and are coming as well, but the first thing I would note is in the last four years we have dramatically increased the interventions on those providers and are now able to take more of them out and stop them playing in the scheme. The commission will talk about how we stop them returning to the scheme as well. But, in the legislation that's currently before parliament, there is a whole range of mid-range capability that we are missing that other regulators or other administrators have. In the legislation before parliament right now there are a range of penalties that would be available to us to apply without having to wait to get through the courts in three, four or five years time. Those penalty provisions can be quite significant—in the tens of thousands of dollars—and that would give us a way to attack the mid-range set of offences. If we can do that early, then we would stop them from graduating into the higher-range offences.

Ms Wade : We have recently received a really important, new set of powers in the integrity and safeguarding act, which came through the parliament in April this year. This has given the commission a stronger and more graduated penalty framework, including new civil penalties, criminal proceedings and higher penalties for aggravated breaches. It now addresses antipromotion orders to restrict marketing practices that exploit participants or undermine the objects of the scheme. It, importantly, expands banning order categories to now capture auditors and consultants. It also provides better protections for whistleblowers and has stronger information-gathering powers. This really does respond to what we have seen in the market over the last decade and what we know to be the behaviour of providers but also brings the commission into alignment with other Commonwealth regulators who respond to these sorts of issues.

Ms Glanville : And just, in particular, in relation to the whistleblower protections, it is important because those protections will very much encourage reporting of suspected fraud, exploitation and unlawful conduct. We figure that will be more apparent from these sorts of powers that we now have, and that's a big plus in terms of addressing the issues that are of concern to you for people with disability.

Senator ROBERTS: I think I know the answer to this question after listening to the previous answers. How will the NDIS ensure that those in genuine need do not lose essential services? It's basically by tightening up the scrutiny and approval of plans, because you don't want to cut off too many people who are entitled to genuine support.

Mr Dardo : The integrity work does not target anyone who's entitled to be on the scheme. And even if somebody who's entitled to be on the scheme may have done something in error or mischievous, that in and of itself does not remove their entitlement to the scheme. We might change the way we manage their plans, but that does not remove their entitlement to the scheme. The integrity work is about optimising what they're entitled to by actually delivering it to them by good providers or through good service systems and making sure they're getting the full value of it. The integrity work is not about reducing what they're entitled to; it's about improving the quality of it.

Mr Comley : Senator, I think your question was about not cutting off people who need it—

Senator ROBERTS: Correct.

Mr Comley : and what they get. The fundamental answer to that is that the bill before the parliament will move to a more consistent test of actual functional capacity—

Senator ROBERTS: A tighter test—

Mr Comley : a tighter test of functional capacity—because, in the establishment of the NDIS, what was established is what's often referred to as access lists based on diagnosis. Those diagnoses are not necessarily well correlated with the support needs that people have. That's probably the most fundamental thing on access. The bill moves to try and tighten up the definition of what are reasonable and necessary supports to ensure that they are provided to those who require them to meet those functional needs.

Mr Dardo : There are a range of things that we would expect a more robust system to be able to do. We have been, over the last four years, building up the system. We've been building the identity-proofing requirements for registered providers that log into our system and make claims. We now require them to log in and—

Senator CAROL BROWN: That's still a small proportion of—

Mr Dardo : It is. But what we can't see in the current system is the flow of funds through the system. So what we can't see is whether those funds are going to a genuine bank account associated with a provider. For unregistered providers or for payments through plan management environments, we can't see the flow of funds going to an end provider.

We would expect that, as we build this system out, we will bring absolute transparency of the whole ecosystem from beginning to end. We would have a way to enrol providers so that we know, whether they're unregistered or registered, that they're a provider that we can attribute an ABN to with confidence. We would be able to connect that ABN to a bank account associated with that provider. We would have confidence that, when we pay a claim, the payment of that claim is transparent to a participant. The participant knows that that claim is being made against their plan, so the participant is agreeing that that service was provided or that those funds should be paid. We would have a mechanism for the system to be able to reconcile that those funds have flowed, the remittances have occurred. We would be able to aggregate up the reporting of all of that and provide transparency of that to the tax system, so the tax system knows where the $45 billion a year is going as well. That's on the integrity of the enrolment and claiming side.

One of the biggest features here is to improve the ease of this for participants—to make it easier for them to pay a provider when they're getting the service, to make it easier for those funds to flow to the provider without the participant being out of pocket and having to reclaim that money from the agency. For an ease of service for genuine providers—providers that are providing genuine services and supports—there's a consistent way for them to provide evidence for those claims so that they know what the expectations are and they know what the channels for the evidence are. They're providing that evidence to us, and we're making payments on the basis of evidence.

If we deliver this well, then what will happen will be that genuine providers will get on a level playing field with the ones that are currently rorting the system. So, instead of genuine providers having to compete with dodgy providers that are not providing real services or that are dodging their tax and super or that are defrauding the scheme without the participants knowing, we would push them out of the market. The genuine providers would be able to reclaim the part of the market that has been compromised, and they'd be able to get a more sustainable business model in play.

Mr Dardo : Absolutely—transparency for them that the money's going to the provider they think it should be going to, transparency for the providers about the flow of funds and transparency to the market that only genuine providers are playing.

Senator CAROL BROWN: And locking out dodgy claims.

Mr Dardo : Yes.

Senator ASKEW: I'm going to go to digital payments now. Mr Dardo : When we develop a program of work, we do what's referred to 'T-shirt sizing' of the types of things we might need to build for that program or work. That T-shirt sizing allows us to identify, roughly, the types of resources and the duration of those resources and have an approximate idea about the type of software or infrastructure we might need. Then, using that material, we develop a costing model. That costing model gives us an estimate of what we need in each year of build and then what we might need in sustainment after that. We have done this before; we did it for Crack Down on Fraud phase 1.

In that T-shirt sizing, there were some offs and ons in terms of the difference between what we did in year 1 and what we did in year 2. We underspent in year 1 and then made that up in year 2. We came in on budget. We came in within the timeframe we said we would build it, and we delivered everything we said we would build. That's been assured by the Digital Transformation Agency, the Department of Finance's gateway reviews and an independent assurer. The teams that did that for Crack Down on Fraud phase 1 are the teams that are working on this concept and have done the T-shirt sizing. Right now, we've worked with DTA to make sure that their assurance is consistent with what we've got in there. As it goes through those normal governance processes, the funds in contingency reserve will be released, and then we'll commence the build.

Senator ASKEW: Going forward, will you have consultants having oversight of the digital system build and the ongoing management of it, or will it be done internally? Will you need to bring in consultants to do that?

We have a program board that sits over the top of it, and that usually includes external agencies. It might be DTA and Finance, and sometimes we need partner agencies that are contributing to the build in some way. There'll be an independent assurer, and we'll procure that. There will be an independent adviser, and we'll procure that. There'll be agency resources that are used—so Public Service resources, APS—and those will be ASL counted resources. Then there will be labour hire resources that will be used because the build is heavily focused on the first two years, so we'll bring workforce on for that. There'll be some subcontractors.

Unusually for government, we are the integrator. I've never delivered a program in 20 years where we've given it to another integrator. We are the integrator. We were the integrator in phase 1 and we'll be the integrator in phase 2. You've got to keep in mind that what we're building here is something that connects the broader systems. It'll connect the banks. It'll provide connections to plan managers or providers. It'll uplift the things that we're able to do in the mobile app. We delivered a new mobile app in the first phase, and we delivered it by bringing it in house and running it. Senator ASKEW: When we were in government, we were working towards a digital system. Is what you've done in the first phase based on that, or is it a whole new digital payment design?

Mr Dardo : I think there have been some previous attempts to do some things. It is not a surprise that, when you're developing a new program and you're bringing an agency together for the first time, there are different ways people may attempt to do it. It is not uncommon for a new program or new agency to be required to use some other agency's platforms, which is what happened initially when the agency was set up. Then it tested the idea that maybe it would bring some providers in to do a build. We've delivered phase 1, and I think we're mature enough to be the integrator now to develop this phase 2. This really is an architecture we will own and run, but it's agnostic of the vendors or the providers. The idea is we own and run the core. Senator ASKEW: Is it a bit like the HICAPS that the doctors and so on use, where it's something completely separate to everybody else, or something like that?

Mr Dardo : The idea of this architecture is that, whether it's high caps or other platforms, depending on what you're trying to achieve over time, they may choose to connect to it. Senator ASKEW: Is that something that we could ask for to be provided on notice?

Mr Dardo : We couldn't do it immediately, but—

Senator ASKEW: Post timeline?

Mr Dardo : Absolutely.

Senator ASKEW: That would be excellent.

Mr Dardo : And I would say we were really transparent with CDOF phase 1. We had a really transparent timeline about what we were doing over a two-year period.

Senator ASKEW: What's the expected end date? Have you got an end timeframe?

Mr Dardo : Most of the build is the next two years, so it's heavily—a lot of the delivery is front loaded, so most of the build is in the next couple of years. Ms Hawke : As you mentioned, the policy intent of the reforms outlined in the legislation in relation to permanence is really to clarify the interpretation of permanence in relation to significant and lifelong disability. As you've referenced in the correspondence that you've just been discussing, that test already exists in the legislation and the current becoming-a-participant rules.

The NDIS review did make it clear that the current legislative framework lacks clarity in relation to how to determine whether an impairment is permanent for the purposes of access. Recommendation 3 of the NDIS review, action 3.9, highlighted this issue and recommended legislative change to strengthen the operation of the permanence criteria.

To address this, part 8 of the bill inserts an approach to assessing permanence of impairments when determining whether a person meets the disability or early intervention requirements and introduces the concept of appropriate treatment. That concept is essentially defined in along three limbs—that a treatment must be evidence based, be reliably expected to improve, reverse or alleviate an impairment and be a treatment that's regularly undertaken in Australia. How the bill will clarify the assessment of permanence is that, essentially, an impairment is not permanent or likely to be permanent unless the person has undertaken all appropriate treatment for their impairment or impairments, and an impairment cannot be found to be permanent if there is other treatment which is likely to materially improve, reverse or alleviate the impact, and to be found permanent, the person's impairment or impairments must be likely to persist for the person's lifetime.

In essence, in relation to your question about access, we have certainly heard community concern that these changes may lead to delays or restrictions to access due to the challenges with treatment availability, and there is an exclusion in relation to consideration of a person's financial and geographical circumstances. The bill does clarify that treatment options need to be considered in the context of recognised clinical practice in Australia, and obviously that includes a range of health systems and services available through Medicare, pharmaceutical benefits and the like, and the evidence that the agency will consider—as they do at the moment—is evidence from treating health practitioners around whether, in fact, there is appropriate treatment available to a person.

Importantly, in relation to consideration of whether an individual is taken to have undertaken all appropriate treatment, there is provision for rules to prescribe circumstances in which a person is taken to have undertaken all appropriate treatment. It's really important that the development of any such rules take into account medical and ethical considerations, such as individual autonomy and informed consent, while establishing system-level parameters around what constitutes reasonable and appropriate treatment. We are looking to use the technical advisory group that was discussed earlier today in the context of developing those rules over the next 12 months, ahead of the 1 January 2028 commencement of that part of the bill, and we expect the consultation process in developing those rules will need to draw on a range of expertise and perspectives, including clinical expertise; lived experience, obviously; consultation with the disability community; input from states and territories; and other consideration of the interaction between the NDIS and health, hospital and rehabilitation systems.

As was the intent of the permanence consideration as part of the assessment of access, obviously the NDIS was never intended to replace treatment and rehabilitation systems, so we have some further important work to do in terms of clarifying the operation of those provisions in the event that the bill passes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: I think what I'm hearing is that the technical advisory group comes first, so I'll go now to the technical advisory group questions and then might come back to the tool. What will be the role of the new technical advisory group?

Ms Wood : I can describe that at a high level. It's broadly, with $3.3 million allocated in the budget, to establish a group to provide expertise on the design of functional capacity assessment tools and instruments. That's their general remit.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: I'm sorry, but could you say that again? I didn't quite hear.

Ms Wood : There was $3.3 million allocated in the budget to establish a technical advisory group. Its basic role is to provide expertise on the design of functional capacity assessment tools and instruments, which is why we won't be doing so until that advice has been given.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Will they, for example, be involved in the determination of the details of the new permanence test?

Ms Wood : They will give advice on how substantially reduced functional capacity can best be measured. Mr Comley : I think what Ms Wood was trying to make clear was just the use of the term 'determined', which makes it sound like it's a decision-making body, whereas it's an advisory body, in the first instance, to the Commonwealth, which then would engage with the states and territories to determine what the rule is that gives effect with the incorporation of the advice, but ultimately it leads to government to decide what is the right tool and what are the right thresholds.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: In this instance, it's 'governments'—

Mr Comley : Governments, yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: from what you've described. So the advice first comes from the group to the Commonwealth, and then, once it has consulted with the Commonwealth, it then goes to the states and territories.

Mr Comley : Yes. Senator STEELE-JOHN: That goes to my next question, which is: who will be on it?

Mr Comley : I'm definitely not going to pre-empt the minister and provide that list, but the intention is people with genuine expertise but also some recognition of the need for lived experience on that group. Expertise and lived experience are the main thing.

Senator McAllister: We would recognise that that group will need input from lived experience, not just by way of membership but also by way of deep consultation with people with expertise, including expertise drawn from lived experience. My confident expectation is that that will be a feature of the tasking from government to the technical advisory group.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Is it correct to say that appointments to the technical advisory group will be appointments made by the minister? Is that functionally or structurally how it works?

Senator McAllister: Yes, I expect so. There may be some other process involved, but essentially yes, upon advice from the department.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Can I clarify, Minister, because there's a slightly different structure in this portfolio space than usual—when we say 'the minister' in this case, are we referring to you, to Minister Butler or to a combination of both of you?

Senator McAllister: We are both involved in the work, but, in the specific question you asked, I expect it will be Mr Butler that makes the appointment.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: You obviously haven't announced the membership of the advisory group at this time. Is there a formal mandate, description of the—

Mr Comley : The terms of reference have not been published.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: When do you intend to publish the terms of reference for the group?

Mr Comley : It's obviously ultimately a matter for the minister, but I would envisage that, at the time the group membership was announced, the terms of reference would probably be announced at the same time.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: You spoke in broad terms, Minister, about the types of people and expertise you'd be looking for. Is there a formal selection criteria for membership of the technical advisory group at this time?

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Have you put together a criteria for membership?

Ms Rule : In short, we conducted a process through a desktop review and also discussed requirements with key stakeholders as well as the department's chief disability adviser. Senator STEELE-JOHN: You mentioned stakeholder groups there. Which stakeholder groups have you consulted with?

Ms Rule : Sorry, I haven't got that list. It's primarily been through either direct representations or existing relationships in the department. As you know, we're in a large department, and there are other chief positions in the department, such as Chief Allied Health Officer and the like.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: You're referring to internal stakeholders.

Ms Rule : It's not only internal, but that's an example. We've had external representations as well, but I don't have a list.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Can you take on notice for us which external stakeholders have been consulted?

Ms Rule : To clarify, we haven't done a consultation process, but we've had representations from people. We have been engaging as people have been reaching out to us, but I want to emphasise that that's not a deciding factor. That is part of—

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Groups have reached out to you.

Ms Rule : They have reached out to us.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: After that process, do you now have a selection criteria that you've been able to provide as advice?

Ms Rule : As I indicated, the selection criteria is technical expertise.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Yes, but do you have a framework that details the type of technical expertise you're talking about there to help guide decision-making?

Ms Wood : Within that framework of technical expertise, there are obviously a range of disciplines that we're aware of that the minister might want to consider that will assist—

Ms Wood : I don't have it in front of me, but we're happy to provide that information to you.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: We'll probably be here for a bit longer, so, if you're able to get it this evening, that would be appreciated. There's no trap, if you like, here. Ms Wood : We've certainly got a list of fields that we're happy to talk to. I wouldn't describe them as selection criteria in a formal sense.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: How will the disability community be consulted on the work of the technical advisory group and the thresholds for functional capacity?

Ms Rule : There are a range of processes we're considering. There will be a formal public consultation process that commences in August and runs until October. We are also considering existing stakeholder reference groups that the department and the agency have, as well as working with the ministers on how we can facilitate a range of different appropriate formats of consultation. I think it would be a similar model potentially to the Thriving Kids Advisory Group, where there's flexibility to talk to a range of experts or stakeholder groups as we develop the products from the technical advisory group.

Mr Comley : I would envisage that one of the first agenda items of the first meeting of the advisory group would be formulating a consultation plan that the members of the advisory group were comfortable with so that they had the right input from the disability community. Ms Hawke : The types of essential expertise that have been identified for the technical advisory group are First Nations diversity assessment; neurodevelopment and/or autism; allied health, preferably occupational therapy and functional needs assessment; paediatric/child development; psychosocial disability/mental health; disability and rehabilitation medicine with expertise in degenerative conditions; assessment, design and statistical expertise; lived experience expertise; and administrative law. Senator STEELE-JOHN: Thank you. I noticed that there's not a reference to chronic illness in that criteria.

Ms Hawke : There's allied health, which would cover chronic illness as well as disability and rehabilitation medicine, including expertise in degenerative conditions.

Mr Comley : As well as general practice, which deals a lot with chronic conditions.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Is what you've just read out there a document that you can table for us?

Mr Comley : I don't think we can table it, because I suspect it's embedded in the advice to the minister. Obviously, it will be in the Hansard, but on behalf of the department I'm happy to offer to extract that information and have it made available to you.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: If you could, that would be great, thank you very much. That's useful. The bill allows for plans to be suspended if a person is not contactable, but the bill does not define what 'non-contactable' actually means. How will it be defined in the implementation of this power?

Ms Hawke : The bill explains: reasonable attempts have been made to contact participants for the purposes of making requests for information or reports under section 36 or section 50. The concept there is 'reasonable attempts'.

Mr Comley : The reason I asked Mr McNaughton to come to the table is I've heard him talk about this before. This part of the bill was an attempt to deal with a very practical administrative practice issue that we face at the moment. I think Mr McNaughton might provide a good bit of colour on this issue.

Mr McNaughton : We'll continue to work with the department on what it looks like as part of this legislation reform, but under the current state we have an 'unable to contact' guideline that we follow. It's usually about making between three and five attempts to contact the participant, in three or five different mediums over a two-week or three-week period. Quite often, we're able to, it's just about convenience, time, multichannel, phone, email letters. If we're still unable to contact that person, in a very small proportion of participants it may be an issue and they're deliberately unable to contact. There could be cultural issues, sensitive issues or the person may be incarcerated, so we have to go through a whole range of strategies around why the person may be unable to be contacted. We have quite a mature process for being unable to contact. We'll work with the department about how we can apply that as part of this new suspension process. We'll continue to work that through, probably building on what we do today.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: That's what we currently do, but my question was, since the bill doesn't define what 'non-contactable' is, how will it be defined as part of the implementation of the legislation? That was my question.

Mr Comley : Ms Hawke may want to comment. The legislation as it stands is the CEO is satisfied that they have made reasonable attempts. Ultimately, it would be, in the first instance, Mr Head forming the guidance of what 'reasonable actions' are. Then, presumably, if somebody wanted to appeal that, they would have their usual appeal rights if they thought it was not, in fact, reasonable.

Mr Head : That's right. What Mr McNaughton has outlined is how we would, in the new world, intend to enliven the process that has been evolved over time and with a lot of experience in the scheme to date.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: So that I understand you, Mr McNaughton talked about three to five contact attempts. Can they be phone calls and other versions of attempted contact, like emails?

Mr McNaughton : We try multimodal attempts in case text, email or letters are a preferred contact method.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: What you're saying, so I don't misunderstand you, is three to five forms of contact are attempted, and then the plan would be suspended—that could be the determination under the legislation?

Mr Head : We would have, as Mr McNaughton outlined, an operational protocol around this.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Okay. So, if a plan is suspended for 90 days, the person's access to the scheme is then revoked. That's another part of the legislation. How will discretion be granted for people who are in hospital, who are overseas or who are not contactable for legitimate reasons out of their control?

Mr Comley : Reading the legislation—and me doing statutory interpretation on the run is very dangerous—clause 40A(8) essentially says, if the 90-day period has come up, the CEO would still have the discretion to take the actions which are in paragraph (4), which is to actually cease the suspension of the plan.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Yes.

ACTING CHAIR: I would just say, if we are getting into that level of line and verse of the legislation, I think that's really the part for next week. We can absolutely look at the policy intent today; it's just that—

Senator STEELE-JOHN: I hear you, Chair. I had drafted these questions with the intent of understanding the intent.

ACTING CHAIR: Before you get to next week.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Well, no—understanding the policy intent as is the purpose of estimates, and then we can go into the further mechanical details. So maybe I'll just do a bit of a verbal reframing. In terms of the policy intent of what we're talking about this evening, what is your department's and your government's policy intent of how to tackle a situation where somebody is non-contactable for legitimate reasons for a period greater than 90 days?

Mr Head : I wouldn't normally jump in on the policy intent, but I think what these provisions do really is provide a more formal framework for dealing with something that can be challenging operationally. But there are a lot of checks and balances in there in terms of providing the CEO with discretion to overturn decisions. So, in a sense, it regularises and authorises a world in which an operating protocol of the type Mr McNaughton articulated can work well and where the CEO is able to exercise discretion in circumstances of the type that you outlined.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Again, staying at the level of intent, if somebody's access to the scheme is unfairly revoked using this power, would they have recourse to challenge the decision or would they need to reapply?

Ms Hawke : It's a reviewable decision.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: So they would be able to seek a review. My office has heard countless examples of NDIS participants who have talked to us about the failure of the agency to meet their communication needs. I'll give you an example. I've spoken to a person who is low vision and who has said that the agency continues to send her documents in formats that can't be read by a screen reader, despite her communicating that she is unable to access them. I wish that this was the first of that specific type of failure that I'd ever encountered, but, in nine years, I can tell you that it isn't. I've lost count of the number of times where that has been brought to me. If someone is deemed uncontactable because the agency repeatedly fails to communicate with them in an accessible way, will they then have their plan suspended?

Ms Hawke : The policy intent is to enable the CEO full discretion in relation to the application of that suspension notwithstanding the period of 90 days.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Using that power, Mr Head, is it your intent to craft a discretionary policy that would take account of situations like that?

Mr Head : Provided it's not inconsistent with the legislation, I think for these sorts of things, particularly where things might go wrong in people's lives or something might happen that disrupts the communication, you would usually have a protocol where there's a set of heads of consideration for how we make the decision so that we're not putting people through onerous processes because of a miscommunication.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: What concerns me is that this participant's recourse would be that they would have to seek a review of this as a reviewable decision. They would have the right to do that, but that's quite an onerous process to go through if it's been the agency's failure that's led them to reach the 90-day period.

Senator McAllister: Indeed. I think the insertion of the word 'reasonable' into the legislation is an indication of the intention.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Okay.

Senator McAllister: It needs to be reasonable.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: It needs to be reasonable. Moving back to the needs assessment simulations that we were discussing earlier, I have a point of clarification there.

Mr McNaughton : While Mr Verlin comes to the table, I took a question on notice to confirm that all 81 of those support needs assessors are allied health qualified.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: All 81 are?

Mr McNaughton : Yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Fantastic. Would you be able to provide us—it would be on notice at this point—their allied health backgrounds.

Mr McNaughton : If I have that level of detail, I will provide that on notice.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: You were describing the process and the experience for participants. You talked about receiving a lot of feedback from participants that this had been a positive experience. They had found the conversations to be useful for them. What is the pathway for a participant to engage in these simulations if they are non-verbal?

Mr Verlin : The support needs assessment will be conducted in any communication mode appropriate for a person with disability. The I-CAN has been used for many years across a number of modes. As part of the testing phase, when we then start to bring in additional cohorts for that testing, we will work through those processes. But we've been really clear that it has to be applied in the most appropriate communication form for the participant.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: So far you've had 290 of these simulations. Have any of them included people that are non-verbal?

Mr Verlin : Not at this stage. Some of the early testing was for cohorts that we were starting to think about for the first transition. Senator STEELE-JOHN: Would you be able to tell us if you've got a target or any other kind of policy in place around the number of non-verbal participants you want to include in your simulations.

Mr Verlin : We haven't got a specific target for particular cohorts. However, it is appropriate, as part of our briefings within the agency and certainly with the department and ministers about providing an appropriate validation and testing program for all cohorts.

Mr Head : I'd add that I have strong oversight of the development of this process. I chair the steering committee with Melbourne university and the Centre for Disability Studies, which has some of the leads in the consortium with senior staff from the agency. The focus on ensuring that the extra time available delivers very significant additional work in the validation space, and the design space is really being ramped up.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: When I asked about the support needs assessment—I think it might have been during the last estimates session, actually; going back a way—I was told that there were additional modules that were being developed for areas that aren't covered by the I-CAN tool in its natural form. I was told that there would be modules for disability health related support, assistive technology, home modifications and behavioural supports. Have these modules been developed, and, if so, what do they look like?

Mr Verlin : We have just completed our first draft of the targeted modules. We've been working with the department on those. They will range depending on the particular module that you've observed. For example, some of the home modifications might be just defining a process on how to get a quote and how to get an assessment. We're building a fair bit on the existing arrangements that occur. However, now that they've been drafted, what we want to do is then start to bring that into the testing. So we'll go beyond the I-CAN and start to do testing on the targeted modules, which then brings additional cohorts into the testing to really work through what the types of questions are or what the additional evidence that we may require is in order to determine the appropriate supports.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: In terms of the process for reviewability, is it correct to say that the review process for these modules will be that they are gradually included into the broader simulations?

Mr Verlin : Correct.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Okay. First of all, can you just confirm for me the modules that are in existence at this point?

Mr Verlin : At this stage, there's assistive technology, disability health related supports, home environments, which is your home modifications and specialist disability accommodation, and behaviour support.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Practically and tangibly, are we talking about documents? Are we talking about videos? What does a module look like in this?

Mr Verlin : More likely documents, but, again, we're just working through, now that we've had a first draft of what those policies are. What we'll then do is really test the form that they are in.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Are you able to table for us the first draft of those documents?

Mr Verlin : I'll need to check with the department.

Mr Comley : Can we take that on notice?

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Take on notice whether you can provide the first draft of those documents. I understand they will be iterative and that draft means it'll change, but it's useful for the committee to know what they look like now. Is there any scope to add additional modules, or are there any additional modules under consideration?

Mr Verlin : Certainly at this stage, what we've done is try to capture all of the supports that there are currently. The CEO has advised that gaps within the testing are also part of the consortium, really understanding as we move away from the core I-CAN—I think we've been really clear that the support needs assessment uses the I-CAN as the basis—that there may be requirements for further modifications as we start to transition more cohorts.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: The start date of new framework planning has been pushed back to April 2027. Is that still the intended start date? Yes? I understand that there will be further consultation on the rules that will underpin the new framework planning process. The last consultation earlier this year went for about six weeks, and we had very little detail for stakeholders to evaluate. Will there be an exposure draft for this new period of consultation?

Ms Rule : We do have a consultation process planned between August and September this year. We're thinking through what the best format is to do that in. I'm not saying no to an exposure draft of the rules. That may come later. The intent of the consultation is to provide far more detail but in simple, plain English, whereas the rules will be very legalistic. We would like to provide that, but I would suggest that's not the next step in consultation, because it won't assist the community to understand them, really. I think the role for us in the next phase is to present detail that has been requested in a way that is plain English, that I can explain and that we don't need a lawyer to explain.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Once that consultation takes place, how will the feedback be incorporated?

Ms Rule : We're working through the consultation at the moment. Part of it will be, as I said, information provision, and then the sorts of things that Ms Hawke and I are thinking about probably do go to that communication element and transition element: How can we work with the community to ensure that we prepare them for the transition? What sort of information do they need? Mr Verlin has touched on this throughout the evening in terms of what he's been discovering through the testing. This is our opportunity to speak to the community about what is a significant transition and, once they've seen more detail, seek their feedback on how we move to implementation.

Mr Comley : To me, this should be a fairly standard consultation process. We take feedback and we decide how much of that's going to be incorporated. I'm a very strong believer that, across our whole portfolio, where we choose not to accept feedback, we should be as transparent as possible about the reasons why we've done that so community members don't feel they have provided input and have no idea where it went. If there is a valid reason that we feel we can't take it up, from a policy perspective, we should be explaining that back to members of the community and stakeholders on the way through.

While I've got the floor and people are watching—I think there are about 280 in the country—it's a general thing I think people should expect of our department that, if we have reservations about their point of view, we should be on the spot to provide that feedback so people then have the opportunity to either clarify their position, which might change, or to go away and think, 'I need a better argument to convince the department and ultimately the government.' I just want to put that on the record.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Thank you. Can I ask about the participant pathway reference group. For clarity, what is the role of this group?

Mr Verlin : We've got a Participant Reference Group, and we've got a participant pathway co-design group. I'm just checking—which group are you referring to?

Senator STEELE-JOHN: It's the participant pathway reference group.

Mr Verlin : We have a Participant Reference Group, and we have a participant pathway co-design group.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: It's the participant pathway co-design group.

Mr Verlin : The intention of our co-design program—we've been running it for well over 12 months now—was to have an opportunity to have formed a group comprised of our disability registered organisations. We had an IAC member and also participants on that. That specific group, the participant pathway group, was the group that we utilised to design the first participant pathway for new framework planning—what would the participant journey be from end to end as part of new framework planning? We did a number of workshops with the group to really set out where we were going to see risks or challenges with the core pathway. We then broke down each one of the moments of that pathway—for example, preparing for a support needs assessment, undertaking the support needs assessment, having the plan discussion with the delegate and then plan implementation. We took each one of those moments and unpacked what the most important things were at that moment for a participant, not from an agency perspective or from a delegate perspective but in terms of what we needed to be mindful of, in doing our design, as part of the pathway. That's been the core intention of the group.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: And they've existed for—

Mr Verlin : Well over 12 months.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: The first group you mentioned, the Participant Reference Group—what is the role of that group? How do you differentiate between them?

Mr Verlin : The Participant Reference Group is a group established by the agency. It was established by our participant advocate. That is a group of about 25 participants, and the agency can use that for any change within the agency. That is a more formal, ongoing group that we can utilise for general agency updates; we can bring particular changes. It's our opportunity, essentially, to have a core group of participants—and carers, I should say. It's not just participants; it's also carers or parents. It's just an additional forum that doesn't have sector representatives or the IAC. It is straight participants.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: And how long has that group existed for?

Mr Verlin : That group has existed for a number of years, and the membership is rotated every 12 to 18 months, with new participants to come on board.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: For the participant pathway co-design group, the one that's existed for the past 12 months, how many times has that group met in that 12-month period?

Mr Verlin : Primarily, it's met monthly. There were times when it was paused when we were holding and seeking additional information from some of the other groups, but our aim initially was monthly. What we have recently done, with the sector organisations last week and with the IAC, is think about how we want to take these groups forward, particularly between now and April. What we want to do is maximise the opportunity. I think the minister has been very clear in recent forums about where the opportunities are to do co-design and do co-design well versus consultation and just broad engagement.

What we want to do is think about one or two moments in that pathway. As we spoke about, there's the design hub, where we're bringing participant insights and changes, and how do we maximise those opportunities? We are doing some thinking about reforming some of the groups as we move forward, particularly between now and April.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: How many times have the Participant Reference Group met this year?

Mr Verlin : I'll take the rhythm on notice. I think it's four or five times a year that they meet. They meet in person for two days. It's a different structure, but I'm happy to take on notice the operating rhythm of the Participant Reference Group.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: If you could, provide how many times they've met in 2026 and the dates of those meetings, as well as how many times they met in 2025 and the dates of those meetings.

Mr Verlin : Certainly.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Thank you. I'll just return briefly to the intent of the bill that's before the parliament at the moment. There's been a lot of conversation about parental responsibility and the changes in the legislation in relation to parental responsibility. Can you explain for us the changes to parental responsibility in the new definition of reasonable and necessary. To clarify, what I'm looking for there is the intent of the changes. I understand we'll go deeper on the bill next week.

Ms Hawke : In effect, the codification of parental responsibility in the bill is, in part, an uplift of some of the criteria that are in the current support rules.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: What do you mean by an uplift?

Ms Hawke : Some of the changes around 'reasonable and necessary' are codifying what's in the act and is already criteria in rules that need to be considered by delegates in determining, for example, what's effective and beneficial, what's value for money and what considerations need to be taken into account in clarifying what is reasonable to expect in terms of the role of families, which is already a criterion and a requirement in the act as part of the determination of reasonable and necessary supports. It's really clarifying what a delegate needs to take into account in making those decisions.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Just so we're on the same page, that's the amendments proposed to the current section 34(1)?

Ms Hawke : Yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: The requirement that parents provide substantial care and support is, I think, the proposed section 34(1)(g)? Okay. When I first looked at these changes, something jumped straight off the page for me personally, and that is within the legislation, as defined at the moment, it talks about parental responsibility, but there is no exception, within the legislation, around the parental responsibility that may be placed on a disabled parent. I'm seeking to understand that I haven't misread or missed a piece of clarification. Is it correct that there is just one definition of parental responsibility? There isn't another clarification around what that might look in the act like for a disabled parent?

Ms Hawke : In relation to consideration of parental responsibility and the principles that are outlined in the legislation, that is considering the supports for a child. Of course, it would be necessary for a delegate to take into consideration that child's and that family's circumstances in making that assessment, but also, relevantly, in relation to a parent with a disability who may also be a participant, there would be relevant considerations in determining what support the parent participant needs in relation to their disability as well.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: I just want to clarify that there is no exception within the NDIS amendment bill to applying parental responsibilities to adult participants, is there?

Ms Hawke : No, that's correct.

Senator McAllister: Sorry, Senator Steele-John, I think we are now again in the territory of going line by line through the application of the legislation. We have tried, over the course of the day, to speak broadly about the reforms and the intents of the reforms, but I do think how the legislation would apply to particular people under particular circumstances starts to really get into the detail of the bill. The chair may assist, but, as I understand it, the reason the Senate observes this rule is because, when the Senate sends a bill to a particular place, the expectation is that the evidence in relation to the bill will largely be heard in that inquiry, not in other forums. Senator STEELE-JOHN: What is the intent for the transitional powers within the bill? They are broad, so I really can only ask you for intent on these.

Mr Comley : If I can be as helpful as possible, this is essentially what is commonly referred to as a Henry VIII clause.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Yes, it is.

Mr Comley : The intent really is, as Ms Hawke commented, that you may have an unintended consequence. In fact, in recent times, things that have come up have been things like whether the IT system that you've built aligns with the way the law has been put together. The idea is a time limited window for 12 months, and then, once you've made it, they're limited to 12 months. So the concept here is that the government would have to come back to parliament to get approval for any change in that law. It just means you don't have unintended consequences. Usually, governments use it when not having that clause would actually disadvantage, in this case, participants in the scheme. That is the primary intention of that clause.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: So I can understand what we have in this backlog of 11,000—they're given an initial assessment; is that how you describe it?

Mr Carracher : That's correct.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: What does that tangibly look like?

Mr Carracher : It's a fairly light touch in terms of looking at the participant safety risk and then looking at risks of breaches of the law and those sorts of things that would mean they need to be dealt with more urgently than some other complaints.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: And a person does this assessment?

Mr Carracher : Yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: And when you say 'light touch', what do you mean?

Mr Carracher : That they're assessing that the participant doesn't have an immediate safety risk that needs to be dealt with or that there isn't a serious breach of rules, or neglect or abuse, that comes through in those complaints.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: How is that done? Is the complaint packaged up in a document, and the document is opened and read?

Mr Carracher : Yes, correct.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: The staff member opens a file up or—what is it?

Mr Carracher : Complaints come to us in a range of ways. Complaints come through the contact centre, where they will hear a matter and push that call through to our complaints intake team. Complaints can come in through emails. Complaints can come in through the web forms. Those three ways are the most common ways we receive complaints. Through those processes, there's that initial assessment we undertake. If there are serious matters that need to be dealt with, particularly safeguarding matters, they will go to our safeguarding team, who will then engage with—it could be other supports in states and territories; it might be police. There could be a range of other services the safeguarding team would engage with in relation to that participant.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: So they're given an initial assessment. Are they then placed in a certain category? You've talked about them being moved to the safeguarding team. Before they end up being transferred in that way, are they given a certain designation?

Mr Carracher : Not at the moment but they will be under the new system, in terms of how we categorise those and move them through the regulatory risk prioritisation model. They're not at this stage.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: At this stage, how are they handled administratively?

Mr Carracher : It's a staff member's assessment of the risks that the complaint presents.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Then the staff member is responsible for forwarding the file or—

Mr Carracher : Within the system, we have a tier 1 and a tier 2 assessment. If at tier 2 a decision is made that it requires regulatory response then it goes through to a panel who assess those matters and then it would be pushed through for regulatory compliance if required.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: At the moment, I'm kind of getting a picture here of why the backlog would have been so large. Of the 11,000 that you have, how many of them have been assessed as containing a risk that means they would need to be moved to the safeguarding team?

Mr Carracher : They will be the ones that haven't got that risk.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: So none of them in that 11,000 bucket have been assessed as having—

Mr Carracher : None have been assessed as having immediate safeguarding or that serious non-compliance.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Because it's so late, can you provide us on notice the framework or the policy documents that guide that assessment of risk so we can have an idea of it? So there's the immediate risk. I hate to be blunt with you but, just so that we're clear, are we talking about a categorisation of risk so we have immediate risk, medium risk low risk?

Mr Carracher : Of the risks that we assess against, serious significant impact on safety and wellbeing and human rights is one criteria. We look at contraventions—breaches—of legislation and rules. Then there's the priority strategic strategy that we're looking at, which depends on if there are matters that we are considering. For example, in the last 12 months we've been looking at meal-time management and dysphagia matters, where participants have been at high risk, and those sorts of things will be also drawn out through that assessment.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: So what you've told us is that, in that 11,000, none of the complaints are in the first category?

Mr Carracher : I'll take that on notice, but my understanding of the process is that that's the assessment.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Could you take on notice to give us a breakdown of your backlog as described, the 11,000, by those three categories that I believe you've stepped us through. I'd like to know the average and the median of the amount of time that people have been waiting for a response, for what you used to describe as first initial contact or something. Do you use the same terminology now? It's been a while since—

Mr Carracher : Yes—the initial contact or engagement.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: It's the one that's not the automatic email reply that you get when you submit.

Mr Carracher : Yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: What do you call it now when an individual actually reaches out to the participant?

Mr Carracher : I don't know if there is a specific name for it, but I will find that out for you.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Is it a check in?

Mr Carracher : Yes, we can call it that.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: If you can tell us the average and median time people have been waiting for that contact, that would be really useful.

Mr Carracher : Sure.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: How many staff does the commission have currently?

Ms Glanville : We gave a senator information about this morning, but I'll just pick it up again. I think it was 957. I might be slightly wrong there.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Have you already given that to Senator Askew?

Ms Sham : Yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: That's great. How many of those staff are allocated to the complaints backlog? We're nearly done, folks.

Ms Sham : We only have the breakdown of allocation for the divisions. Within our complaints and engagement division, there are 265 staff. Not all of them, though, would be working on the backlog matters, as Mr Carracher mentioned. There are some dedicated staff related to that, which we can take on notice. We can give you a bit of a breakdown of what staff are working on the tiers, which we described around the first line of assessment, and then escalation through to the regulatory process where required.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Within your different sections or different types of staff, have you got different KPIs for those working within different areas or one KPI across the whole? I believe there's a complaints resolution KPI on people within the complaints-handling team. Is that correct?

Mr Carracher : For the individual staff, how many they need to do?

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Yes. How many they've got to get—

Mr Carracher : No, we don't have that.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Do you have an organisational—I guess a KPI might not be the right word—target of reaching 70 per cent complaint resolution within a certain time frame?

Mr Carracher : Yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: What's the time?

Ms Sham : Seventy per cent within 90 days is within performance measures.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Within 90 days is your performance measure. Do you believe there are additional staff needed to reach that target, or do you feel you're now staffed at an appropriate level to get there?

Ms Glanville : I think a really important piece of this—and they're really good questions—is to look at our systems issues. This is why DART is so important to us—for example, many of our staff currently have to manually input data to this work, DART will assist us to have this populated and will enable staff to actually spend more time doing the critical work that you're talking about as distinct from putting things together manually. This is also the case when we're looking at perhaps more complicated issues and where there might be particular safeguarding needs. Our systems across the agency don't intersect. That means that staff have to manually pull out data. If complaints come in about a provider, for example, and our staff want to see what contact points we've had with this provider, they have to manually do that work at the moment.

Ms Sham is leading the work on DART. I'm very happy to report we had our first internal launch last week of prepopulating registration, so our staff don't have to go in and do all that. They don't have to go through systems that are disconnected to find these touch points, so their ability to look at something and make a risk assessment will be incredibly enhanced by these shifts and changes. It might sound like we're focusing on that a lot, but it is a hugely positive frame for us, and it will really help us move forward much more thoroughly in better using the material we have to not just deal with individual matters but to look at systemic issues that we're seeing in the market and to be able to take different sorts of action or perhaps, as Mr Carracher mentioned previously, campaigns of some sort or to look at what learning needs to be there.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: This is my last question, I think, because I've figured out how to turn three into one. Have you done any projections in relation to potential increased workload as a result of either the legislative reforms more broadly or the shift to mandatory registration specifically?

Ms Sham : This morning, I gave evidence around the breakdown of additional staffing and funding that was provided in the expansion of mandatory registration. One component of that is the ongoing regulatory activities, which we expect to increase. For example, as more providers are registered, there'll be more reportable incidents that they are required to report—equally our level of oversight and then intervention—throughout the registration period. Oversight and interventions would increase as a result of those providers being registered.

As Ms Glanville said, at the moment the new systems that will be supported through the rollout of DART will significantly reduce the amount of manual intervention that our staff have to experience every day in all aspects of the commission's roles, from complaints all the way through to taking a regulatory intervention. By removing a lot of those manual processes, we then expect to be able to uplift the number of activities that we're delivering in the staffing complement we have but also turn our focus to the increased numbers through mandatory registration.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Could you take on notice for me to provide information to the committee outlining the—is it DART?

Ms Sham : Data and Regulatory Transformation, DART. Yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: DART. Oh Lord! Could you provide us on notice an outline of that program or any briefing papers you are able to provide on that for us to understand what that change means for the commission, what it may mean for the people contacting my office and what they can then expect in terms of their experience with the commission. That would be really useful.

Ms Sham : Yes.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Thank you.
